meta.reviewer_notes: The catalogue has ooo-0045 ("the journey rather than the destination is the thing a pilgrimage performs"); this passage does not assert that, it tests it against evidence: what pilgrims did with the railways, and the fact that the reinvented hardships are bounded and elected. The payload is the concession, which hands the first view the argument and takes away part of the prize. The near-tie is in Q4, between a concession that narrows a verdict and a withdrawal of it, decided by "the first view wins the argument about what the hardship was". The voice is measured and long-sentenced (the highest sentence mean in the batch), with one short scene in the clerk's office and the nineteenth century named. The move is adjudication with a concession that bounds the conclusion, and the voice is measured, long-sentenced, with one short scene at the opening.

quality.adversarial_review: Q1: A strong candidate argues for the hostels-and-churches option because those are the words in the sentence; "satisfied that the person in front of her has walked at least the last hundred kilometres" names what is being checked, and the stamps are only how. Q2: The tour-company option tempts as a debunking, and a careful candidate may object that the rationing option attacks only the Santiago example; but it is the only option that lets the second view explain the evidence (walking as the price of an object got at the place), while the others are irrelevant, strengthening, or beside the point, and the Santiago minimum is the author's lead example. Q3: The suffer-less option is argued from the telephone and the bounded cost; "the cost is real" and "bounded and elected" make a claim about kind, not amount, and the account would survive if the new walk were harder, so the option is not necessary. Q4: The withdrawal option is the near-tie; "the first view wins the argument about what the hardship was" is the sentence that keeps the verdict, and "loses something in the winning" is the narrowing, not a reversal.

paragraphs.text: In a small office beside the cathedral at Santiago de Compostela a clerk reads the inked stamps of hostels and parish churches in a booklet and counts backwards along the route until satisfied that the person in front of her has walked at least the last hundred kilometres, the distance the cathedral requires for its certificate of pilgrimage. The pilgrim could have come the whole way by train, and most of the queue came most of the way on wheels, but the certificate is not for arriving. It is for the hundred kilometres, and the queue is long.

Two accounts of why pilgrimage is hard are on offer. On the first, the hardship is the point: blistered feet and an empty stomach are a cost, and a cost is what proves to the pilgrim and to the community left behind that the journey was in earnest. On the second, the hardship was never more than the price of distance. Before railways a shrine was far and the road dangerous, so devotion paid in weeks of walking as a merchant paid, and the holy ground at the end was always the object; the suffering was no more sacred than the mud. The second view has the attraction of modesty, and the nineteenth century seemed to confirm it: when the railways came the shrines did not empty but filled. Special trains carried the sick to Lourdes from the 1870s, and the route to Santiago, down to a few hundred walkers a year, now receives hundreds of thousands.

But look at what the arrivals did with the ease they were given: they refused a part of it, consistently. Where the train took them to the door they got off early and walked the last stretch, and the walking was then codified, as at Santiago, into a minimum. Where the road was smooth they chose an older path that was not. Where the journey no longer tired the body, it was tired on arrival by other means: an all-night vigil, a fast, a climb made barefoot over stones. If arriving at the place were all that mattered, the train would have been accepted without remainder, as the merchant accepted it. An institution that keeps its difficulty after the reason for it has gone is telling you what the difficulty was for, and the destination view cannot read the message.

Still, the hardship that was reinvented is not the hardship that was lost. The old pilgrim did not choose the distance; it was simply there, with the bandits and the fevers, and its cost was open-ended in a way no vigil is. The new pilgrim chooses the hundred kilometres, knows to the hour when they will end, carries a telephone and could stop at any town. The cost is real, but it is bounded and elected, and a bounded, elected cost cannot prove what an unbounded, imposed one proved. It no longer shows the community that you faced what the world put in your way, since the world put nothing there. It shows, mostly to yourself, that you were willing to put something there. So the first view wins the argument about what the hardship was, and loses something in the winning: the certificate the modern pilgrim carries out of the clerk's office attests a willingness, not an endurance, and those are different virtues.

questions.target_mistake: taking the evidence the clerk reads (stamps from hostels and churches) for the thing she is checking, or extending the requirement to the whole route
questions.stem: According to the passage, the clerk at Santiago is checking that the pilgrim

options.A: travelled the whole route without using a train
options.B: covered at least the final hundred kilometres on foot
options.C: stayed at the hostels and parish churches named along the route
options.D: completed the journey within the time the cathedral allows

explanation.expert_notice: The sentence says what she must be "satisfied" of: "that the person in front of her has walked at least the last hundred kilometres, the distance the cathedral requires". The stamps are how she checks; the hundred kilometres is what.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option states the requirement as the passage gives it: at least the final hundred kilometres, on foot. The next sentence confirms that the rest of the route may be done by train: "the certificate is not for arriving. It is for the hundred kilometres."
explanation.question_type_note: A detail question on a scene often separates the method of checking from the thing checked. Ask what the clerk needs to be true, not what she is looking at.
explanation.reading_habit: When a passage says "at least the last X", the requirement is X, not the whole. Options that enlarge "the last" to "the whole" are scope traps.

distractors.why_wrong: the pilgrim could have come the whole way by train, and the certificate "is not for arriving"
distractors.seductive_element: the scene is about walking, so a reader assumes the walking must be total

distractors.why_wrong: the "inked stamps of hostels and parish churches" are the evidence she reads, not the requirement; she "counts backwards along the route" to a distance
distractors.seductive_element: the option uses the sentence's own nouns, which makes it feel like recall

distractors.why_wrong: no time limit appears anywhere in the passage
distractors.seductive_element: certificates usually have conditions of time, and "knows to the hour when they will end" appears later

questions.target_mistake: picking a statement that is merely unflattering to pilgrims, or one the author has already conceded, instead of one that lets the second view explain the evidence
questions.prediction_target: the argument is that reinvented hardship cannot be explained by the destination view; a weakener gives the destination view a way to explain it, for instance by showing the walking is the price of something obtained at the destination
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument against the second view?

options.A: Numbers at the shrines the railways reached rose far more steeply than numbers at shrines they never reached.
options.B: Walkers on the Spanish route describe the final stretch as the most meaningful part of the whole journey.
options.C: Most of those who walk the final hundred kilometres do so in groups arranged for them by tour companies.
options.D: The cathedral set the minimum to ration certificates, and most walkers say they walk only to get one.

explanation.expert_notice: The author's blow against the second view is one sentence: "If arriving at the place were all that mattered, the train would have been accepted without remainder." The evidence is that pilgrims chose hardship the journey no longer required. To weaken it, show that the chosen hardship is after all about arriving, or about getting something at the place.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option does that. If the minimum was set to ration certificates and walkers walk only to get one, then the walking is the price of an object handed out at the destination, which is exactly the shape of the second view: a cost paid to reach something at the place, "no more sacred than the mud". The author's central example would then not show what the author needs it to show.
explanation.question_type_note: A weaken question asks which statement, if true, loosens the link between the author's evidence and the author's conclusion. Name the link first (chosen hardship shows that hardship was the point), then look for the option that explains the same evidence without the conclusion.
explanation.reading_habit: The strongest weakener often re-describes the author's own example from the rival's side. Ask of each option: does this let the view under attack explain the evidence after all?

distractors.why_wrong: the author already grants that the railways filled the shrines ("the shrines did not empty but filled"); the argument is about what pilgrims did with the ease, not how many came
distractors.seductive_element: numbers are the second view's evidence in paragraph two, so more of them feels like more for the second view

distractors.why_wrong: if the walking is "the most meaningful part", the hardship is being valued for itself, which is the author's claim, not the second view's
distractors.seductive_element: it is about the last stretch, the author's example, and sounds like fresh evidence about it

distractors.why_wrong: who organises the walking does not touch whether the hardship is chosen for its own sake; a group still walks
distractors.seductive_element: tour companies make the walk sound commercial and therefore not devotional, which feels like a point against the author

questions.target_mistake: choosing a statement that is probable or in the passage's spirit rather than one the account cannot do without
questions.prediction_target: the account rests on pilgrims refusing part of the ease they were given; if nobody chose hardship they did not need, there would be nothing to explain, so that at least some do is necessary
questions.stem: If the author's account is correct, which of the following must be true?

options.A: Some pilgrims who could reach a shrine without hardship choose hardship anyway.
options.B: Pilgrims in the railway age suffer less than pilgrims before it did.
options.C: The community left behind no longer takes any interest in a pilgrim's journey.
options.D: Shrines the railway never reached lost their pilgrims to shrines it did.

explanation.expert_notice: The third paragraph's premise is stated as fact: "they refused a part of it", got off the train early, "chose an older path", fasted, climbed barefoot. The whole argument is an inference from this. Anything the argument stands on must be true if the account is correct; the rest is what the author adds on top.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that premise in minimal form, with "some". Without at least some pilgrims choosing hardship they could avoid, there is no reinvented difficulty and nothing for the first view to win. The option claims nothing about how many or why.
explanation.question_type_note: A must-be-true question rewards the weakest option that the passage cannot do without. Prefer "some" to "all", and a premise the argument rests on to a consequence the author merely suggests.
explanation.reading_habit: Ask of each option: if this were false, would the author's argument collapse? Only the answer passes. Options about degree, comparison or other shrines fail the test even when they sound true.

distractors.why_wrong: the author says the new cost is "bounded and elected", not smaller; "the cost is real"
distractors.seductive_element: bounded sounds like less, and the passage contrasts bandits and fevers with a telephone

distractors.why_wrong: "it shows, mostly to yourself" leaves room for the community; "no longer takes any interest" turns "mostly" into "entirely"
distractors.seductive_element: the final paragraph does move the proof from the community to the self

distractors.why_wrong: the passage says nothing about shrines the railway never reached
distractors.seductive_element: it is the kind of thing that would follow if arriving were all that mattered, which is the view the author rejects

questions.target_mistake: reading a concession that bounds a conclusion as a retraction of it, or missing that the paragraph changes the conclusion at all
questions.prediction_target: the paragraph opens with "Still", grants a difference between old and new hardship, and ends by saying the first view "wins ... and loses something in the winning": it qualifies the verdict without reversing it
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the function of the final paragraph?

options.A: It withdraws the author's support for the first view in the light of a counterexample it cannot answer.
options.B: It gathers the evidence of the previous paragraph and restates its conclusion in stronger terms than before.
options.C: It concedes that the new hardship differs from the old, and narrows what the first view's victory shows.
options.D: It introduces a third view, on which modern pilgrimage proves nothing at all, and endorses that view.

explanation.expert_notice: "Still" at the opening signals a concession. The body gives the difference: the old cost was "open-ended", the new one "bounded and elected". The last sentence keeps the verdict and limits it: "the first view wins the argument about what the hardship was, and loses something in the winning". That is a narrowing, not a reversal.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option names both halves: the concession (new differs from old) and the narrowing (what the victory shows is "a willingness, not an endurance"). The verdict for the first view is kept in the same sentence that limits it.
explanation.question_type_note: A paragraph-function question on a closing paragraph is a test of whether you can tell a qualification from a retraction. Read the first word and the last sentence: "Still" plus "wins ... and loses something" is a qualification.
explanation.reading_habit: When a final paragraph begins with "still", "yet" or "but", find the sentence that says what survives. If the author's verdict survives in bounded form, the paragraph's function is to bound it, not to withdraw it.

distractors.why_wrong: "the first view wins the argument about what the hardship was" keeps the author's support; what changes is what the win covers
distractors.seductive_element: the paragraph is full of differences between old and new hardship, which read like objections

distractors.why_wrong: the paragraph adds a new distinction, bounded against open-ended, rather than restating; it ends by saying the first view "loses something", the opposite of stronger terms
distractors.seductive_element: closing paragraphs usually summarise, so a reader expects one

distractors.why_wrong: the certificate "attests a willingness, not an endurance", which is a different proof, not no proof
distractors.seductive_element: "cannot prove what an unbounded, imposed one proved" sounds like proof has failed altogether

vocabulary.passage_use: the walking was then codified, as at Santiago, into a minimum

vocabulary.meaning_here: completely, with nothing left over or held back

mentor.challenge: Trains reach the shrine. Pilgrims get off early and walk the last stretch anyway, then queue to prove they did. Why keep a hardship that nobody needs any more?
mentor.one_sentence_summary: A clerk at Santiago checks that pilgrims walked at least the final hundred kilometres even though trains could carry them the whole way, which the passage uses to argue that modern pilgrims' deliberately kept hardships show that hardship itself, not just arrival, was always part of the point, though the chosen, bounded hardship of today proves a different and lesser thing than the open-ended hardship it replaced.
mentor.main_idea: Because modern pilgrims who could easily reach a shrine by train still choose to walk, fast, or climb barefoot, the view that pilgrimage hardship was only ever the price of distance cannot explain the evidence; hardship itself was part of the point. But because today's hardship is chosen and has a known end, while the old hardship was simply imposed, the modern version proves only a willingness to suffer, not the endurance the old pilgrims actually showed.
mentor.simple_explanation:
In an office next to the cathedral at Santiago de Compostela, a clerk reads the stamps collected in a pilgrim's booklet from hostels and parish churches along the way, checking backwards until she is satisfied the person in front of her walked at least the final hundred kilometres, which is the distance the cathedral requires for its certificate. The pilgrim could have taken a train the whole way, and most of the people in the queue did travel most of the way by train, but the certificate is not given for simply arriving. It is given for that hundred kilometres on foot, and the queue for it is long.

Two explanations for why pilgrimage has always been hard are on offer. The first says the hardship itself is the point, since blistered feet and hunger are a cost that proves to the pilgrim, and to the people left at home, that the journey was taken seriously. The second says the hardship was never more than the price you had to pay to cover the distance, since before railways a shrine was far away and the road was dangerous, so devotion simply cost weeks of walking the way a trader's goods cost weeks of travel, and the holy destination was always the real goal, with the suffering along the way no more meaningful than mud on a boot. This second view looked right in the nineteenth century, since when railways arrived the shrines did not empty out, they filled up: special trains carried the sick to Lourdes from the 1870s, and the Santiago route, once down to a few hundred walkers a year, now gets hundreds of thousands.

But look closely at what pilgrims actually did with the easier journey the trains gave them: again and again, they turned down part of it. Where a train would take them right to the door, they got off early and walked the final stretch anyway, and that walking eventually became an official minimum, as at Santiago. Where the road had become smooth, many chose a rougher, older path instead. Where the journey itself no longer tired the body, pilgrims tired themselves by other means instead, an all-night vigil, a fast, or a barefoot climb over stones. If simply arriving at the shrine were all that ever mattered, pilgrims would have accepted the train completely, the way a trader accepts a faster route without objection. The fact that an institution keeps its difficulty even after the original reason for that difficulty has disappeared is telling you what the difficulty was actually for, and the destination-only view has no way to explain that.

Still, the hardship that pilgrims reinvented for themselves is not quite the same hardship that was lost. The old pilgrim never chose the distance; it was simply there, along with bandits and fevers, and its cost had no fixed end the way a modern vigil does. The new pilgrim instead chooses the hundred kilometres, knows exactly when it will end, carries a telephone, and could stop in any town along the way. That cost is real, but it is both bounded and freely chosen, and a cost like that cannot prove the same thing an unbounded, imposed cost once proved. It no longer shows the community back home that you faced whatever the world happened to put in your path, since the world put nothing there this time. It shows, mostly just to yourself, that you were willing to put something difficult there on purpose. So the first view, that hardship itself is the point, wins the argument about what the difficulty was for, but loses something even in winning: the certificate a modern pilgrim carries out of that clerk's office proves a willingness, not an endurance, and those two things are not the same virtue.
mentor.why_difficult: The passage's final move is a concession that narrows its own conclusion rather than reversing it, and readers who expect a closing paragraph to either fully agree or fully disagree with what came before can easily mistake that careful narrowing for either a full retraction or an unqualified victory.
mentor.author_intention: To use what pilgrims actually did once trains made travel easy as evidence that hardship itself, not just arrival, was always part of pilgrimage, while also being honest that the modern, chosen version of that hardship proves a more limited thing than the old, imposed version did.

paragraph_journey.note: A clerk at Santiago checks that a pilgrim walked the last hundred kilometres on foot, even though the rest of the journey could be done by train.
One view says hardship itself was always the point of pilgrimage, and the other says it was only ever the price of distance, which railways seemed to confirm by filling the shrines anyway.
What pilgrims actually did once trains made travel easy, getting off early, choosing rough paths, inventing new hardships, shows that hardship itself was part of the point after all.
The new, chosen hardship is not the same as the old, imposed one, so the first view wins the argument but proves a smaller thing, willingness rather than endurance.

mentor.tone_progression: The voice stays measured and quietly admiring throughout, opening on one concrete scene in a clerk's office and building, through long, careful sentences, to a conclusion that is granted and limited in the same breath.
key_transitions: 'But look at what the arrivals did with the ease they were given: they refused a part of it, consistently.' (opening of paragraph 3): the passage turns from reporting two views to testing them against evidence.
'Still, the hardship that was reinvented is not the hardship that was lost.' (opening of paragraph 4): the concession begins.
'So the first view wins the argument about what the hardship was, and loses something in the winning...' (closing paragraph 4): states the narrowed verdict the whole passage has been building toward.
mentor.misunderstanding: A hurried reader treats the final paragraph as either cancelling the argument for the first view or simply repeating it more strongly, missing that it does a third thing: it keeps the verdict for the first view while narrowing exactly what that verdict is allowed to prove.
mentor.traps_summary: The wrong options take evidence that genuinely weakens the author's position only in the same debunking direction as everything around it, confuse what the destination view cannot explain with what it can, mistake a comparison of kind for a comparison of amount, or read a bounding concession in the closing paragraph as either a full withdrawal or a mere restatement.
mentor.reading_lesson: When a closing paragraph opens with a word like 'still' or 'yet', look for a sentence near the end that tells you what survives from before; a verdict can be kept and narrowed in the very same sentence, and that is different from both agreeing fully and taking it back.
mentor.real_world: The same pattern appears whenever an old constraint is removed but people voluntarily recreate a version of it, such as runners choosing hard routes once cars make travel effortless, or fasting kept as a chosen discipline once famine is no longer a real threat.
mentor.takeaway: A chosen, bounded hardship can prove that someone was willing to suffer, but it cannot prove the same thing an unchosen, open-ended hardship once proved.
mentor.reflection_question: Can you think of a difficulty you keep by choice today that other people once faced only because they had no way to avoid it?

eli10.big_idea: Even though trains can carry pilgrims all the way to a shrine, many choose to walk the last part anyway, which shows that the hard part was always meant to matter, not just getting there.
eli10.story: A train can take a pilgrim almost all the way to a famous shrine. But many pilgrims get off early anyway and walk the last stretch on foot. At one shrine, you can only get an official certificate if you walked at least the last hundred kilometres. Why bother, if a train could take you the whole way? Some people say the hard walk never really mattered, only reaching the shrine mattered. But if that were true, everyone would simply ride the train all the way. Instead, people get off early, pick harder paths, or even climb barefoot over stones. That shows the hard part really was part of the point all along. Still, there is a difference. Long ago, the hard journey was forced on pilgrims by a dangerous world. Today, pilgrims choose their hardship, and they know exactly when it will end. So today's hard walk proves something smaller. It shows a pilgrim is willing to suffer, not that they truly endured whatever came their way.
paragraphs: A clerk checks that a pilgrim walked the final hundred kilometres, even though a train could have gone all the way.
One view says hardship itself was the point of pilgrimage, and another says it was only ever the price of a long journey.
What pilgrims did once trains made things easy, choosing hardship anyway, shows the first view is right.
Today's chosen hardship is different from the old forced kind, so it proves willingness, not true endurance.
eli10.author_view: The writer admires what modern pilgrims do but stays careful and precise, giving the first view the win while being honest about exactly how much smaller that win really is.
